definition: There are many applications of virtual reality (VR).
details: Applications have been developed in a variety of domains, such as architectural and urban design, industrial designs, restorative nature experiences, healthcare and clinical therapies, digital marketing and activism, education and training, engineering and robotics, entertainment, virtual communities, fine arts, heritage and archaeology, occupational safety, as well as social science and psychology. Virtual Reality (VR) is revolutionizing industries by enabling immersive, interactive simulations that greatly improve the work of professionals in these industries. VR is changing how experts approach problems and come up with creative solutions in a variety of fields, including architecture and urban planning, where it helps visualize intricate structures and simulate entire cities, and healthcare and surgery, where it enhances accuracy and patient safety. As evidenced by successful collaborative operations using VR platforms, advancements in VR enable surgeons to train in risk-free environments and sketch out treatments customized for particular patients. explainer.lead: Virtual reality has been applied across design, healthcare, education, engineering, entertainment, heritage and other domains. It matters because immersive, interactive simulation lets these fields test and train in conditions hard or costly to reproduce in reality.

tiers.eli5: It's like putting on special goggles that make you feel inside a computer-made place, and people use that for everything from designing buildings to practising surgery.
tiers.practitioner: Teams build VR applications per domain—for example clinical therapy scenarios or design walkthroughs—rather than one general-purpose product. A common pitfall is treating immersion as the goal instead of fit to the task and its users.
tiers.paperLevel: No single formal definition is given; VR applications are characterized by immersive, interactive simulation deployed in a range of domains. Limits are domain-specific: suitability depends on the simulation being able to represent the relevant conditions faithfully.

explainer.example: An architectural team uses a VR application to let clients walk through an urban design before construction, and a clinical team uses one for a therapy scenario.
